newsitem.title: UK: UK GDP data strengthen case for rates on hold.
newsitem.headline: UK GDP data strengthen case for rates on hold.

text.p: Third quarter GDP data showed UK growth is gathering pace, but Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke can still argue there is little danger of a boom and interest rates should stay on hold.

"The figures show although the economy is growing at a strong pace there is no hint of a boom. They should give Clarke enough leeway to leave rates on hold next week," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.
The data showed GDP grew 0.8 percent in the third quarter for year-on-year growth of 2.3 percent.
The figures showed the service sector was again the star performer, growing 0.9 percent in the quarter for a year-on-year rate of 3.3 percent.

Cates said the Clarke will also be able to argue that despite the surge in consumer demand there is no evidence it is sucking in excessive levels of imports. "The export performance is very good and although imports are growing strongly there is no sign the consumer sector is overheating," said Cates.
Other figures showed the trade gap between Britain and the rest of the world improved dramatically in August, narrowing to 584 million stg in August from 1.22 billion stg in July.

Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank America, agreed the Chancellor will use the GDP figures to argue for rates on hold. "The rise in GDP should constitute the final nail in the coffin of rate cut hopes, but it will certainly not be deemed strong enough by Clarke to justify a tightening."
But with the economy now growing roughly at trend, the latest figures will intensify debate about how much faster it can grow without sparking higher inflation.
"We doubt there is enough spare capacity left to allow a near term fall in inflation," said Marion Bell, Treasury economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland.
Cates agrees. "Using capacity utilisation figures from the CBI and real earnings data our view is that there is very little spare capacity left."

He said the growth in real earnings is of particular concern. The tax and price index rose by just 0.6 percent in the year to August, so real earnings growth was close to the 4.0 percent rise in average earnings.

More up-to-date but incomplete trade figures showed exports to countries outside the EU dropped slightly in September, but analysts said there was no reason to assume sterling's recent appreciation is having an impact just yet.

"It's always difficult to work out how much is to do with appreciation and how much to do with weakness overseas. I think in this case it's more to do with slower growth overseas, especially in the U.S.," said Hawkins.
The trade gap between the UK and countries outside the EU widened to 851 million stg in September from 597 million stg in August.

The export volume index slipped to 135.6 from 136 in August. Longer-term measures showed in the three months to September exports grew by 2.0 percent compared with 3.0 percent in the three months to August.
grew The pound has appreciated by more than 5.0 percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August.
The Confederation of British Industry said this week that, so far, the pound's rally has not hurt its exporting members.
"If the CBI is not complaining, it probably means the pound can go a bit further still without causing too much hardship," said Hawkins. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
